amendments.rule: An English particle or adverb that realizes a Greek **preverb** rides inside the compound verb's own unit and is never `added`, as a discontinuous realization under rule 15 where the ASV separates them: `ἐξῆλθεν` → *went forth*, `ἐξέβαλον` → *cast out*, `ἀνέβη` → *went up*, `ἐπεβίβασαν` → *set thereon* at LUK.19.35, `προσηργάσατο` → *hath made more* at LUK.19.16, `ἀπολάβωσιν` → *receive again* at LUK.6.34. The head is the English word glossing the **verbal root**, never the particle. The corpus is unanimous: 963 units across 141 chapters carry such a particle and every one of them is `aligned`, none `added`, and the head stands on the verb word in all but one class. This is scoped to a particle **no other source token stands to answer to**. Where an expressed preposition does answer to it — because the particle is part of that preposition's own English gloss, as *out* is of `ἐκ` → *out of* — the whole English prepositional expression is the preposition's, headed on the prepositional word, and the compound verb keeps only its verb word: `ἔξελθε ἐξ αὐτοῦ` → *come* and *out of*, `ἐξῆλθεν ἐξ αὐτοῦ` → *came* and *out of*, as `εἰσελθὼν εἰς` → *entered* and *into* and `ἀπῆλθεν ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ` → *departed* and *from* do. Rule 36 is what decides that and says it in terms: an English preposition governing a prepositional phrase realizes the Greek preposition and not the verb it depends on, even where English idiom makes the verb phrasal, and a preposition is left `unrepresented` only where English realizes it nowhere at all — so do not leave such a preposition a bare *of* while the verb takes the *out*. That arm is scoped to where the ASV writes **one** English particle for the two, and the count of English words the ASV wrote is what decides it, as rule 94 decides a compound unit by that same test. Where the ASV writes a particle for the preverb **in addition to** a complete prepositional expression, each token takes its own and the verb does not go bare: `Ἔξελθε … ἐκ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου` → *Come forth* and *out of the man* gives *forth* to the imperative and *out of* to `ἐκ`, as `τὴν ἐξ αὐτοῦ δύναμιν ἐξελθοῦσαν` → *the power proceeding from him had gone forth* gives *forth* to the participle and *proceeding from* to `ἐξ`. That the preverb and the preposition are the same morpheme is not the test and does not strand the extra word: this rule's own count forbids marking such a particle `added`, and rule 36 forbids handing it to a preposition whose English is already complete, so the verb is the only token left to take it. A **noncompositional prepositional phrase** standing in the same clause answers to the particle in the same way, and the single English word is that phrase's rather than the preverb's: `συνήχθησαν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό` → *were gathered together* gives *were gathered* to the verb and *together* to `ἐπί` + `αὐτό` as one `noncompositional` unit under rule 45, the intervening article standing `unrepresented` under rule 93, as MAT.22.34 and ACT.4.26 read it and as ACT.2.44 reads the same phrase where no compound verb competes. Where no such phrase stands, the preverb keeps the word in the ordinary way, which is why `συνηγμένοι` → *gathered together* and `συνήχθησαν` → *were gathered together* keep *together* inside the verb's own unit. A preverb whose sense the following preposition's gloss does **not** carry keeps this rule's ordinary treatment, which is why `ἀναβαίνων ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος` → *coming up out of the water* gives *up* to the participle and *out of* to `ἐκ` in one clause, and why `ἐκβάλλει … εἰς` → *driveth … forth* and *into* does. Rule 94 decides only whether the preposition and the word it governs form one unit, and does not decide where the particle goes. Where the compound verb governs a bare dative or genitive that the ASV writes with an English preposition, that preposition realizes the case government and rides with the governed word under rules 21, 36 and 69, as MRK.14.65 has it and as ACT.4.1 `ἐπέστησαν αὐτοῖς` → *came* and *upon them* and ACT.4.3 `ἐπέβαλον … αὐτοῖς` → *laid* and *on them* do. That arm too is scoped to where the ASV writes an English **verb word of its own** for the compound, as *came* and *laid* are. Where it writes none, and the English preposition is the only word carrying the compound's lexical sense, the preposition stays inside the verb's unit and the governed word takes its bare pronoun or noun: `προϊσταμένους ὑμῶν` → *are over* and *you* gives *are over* to the participle headed on *over* and a bare *you* to the genitive, `προΐστημι` meaning to stand before while *are* is only the periphrastic copula. Rule 17 is what forces this, forbidding a head on a subject or an auxiliary: a unit stripped to *are* would have no lexical word left to head on, whereas the governed word loses nothing, its case being what the verb's own sense already expresses. 1TH.5 writes both arms, giving *upon them* to the dative of `ἐφίσταται` → *cometh upon them* and keeping *over* with the participle of `προϊσταμένους`, which is what shows that an English verb word standing for the compound, and not the case the verb governs, is what decides. The one exception is an idiom that leaves no English verb word to head on at all: `Ἆρον` → *away with him* at JHN.19.15 and `Αἶρε` → *away with* at LUK.23.18 head on *away*, because nothing else was written.
amendments.why: Rule 106's case-government arm is stated without a precondition, but all three of its cited precedents (MRK.14.65, ACT.4.1 ἐπέστησαν αὐτοῖς → *came* / *upon them*, ACT.4.3 ἐπέβαλον αὐτοῖς → *laid* / *on them*) write an English verb word of their own, so the arm has never been tested against a compound whose only lexical English word is the preposition. 1TH.5 supplies both arms in one chapter: 5.3 matches the precedent exactly, and 5.12 προϊσταμένους ὑμῶν → *are over you* does not, because obeying the arm as written would strip *over* to the genitive and leave the participle a bare *are*, which rule 17 forbids as a head. Returned as an amendment rather than a new rule because the over-broad sentence is inside rule 106 itself and a cross-reference elsewhere would leave it to be read first.

conventions: A compound verb governing a bare dative or genitive is decided by whether the ASV writes an English verb word of its own for it. 1TH.5.3 ephistatai autois -> *cometh* / *upon them* gives the preposition to the governed dative under rule 106's case-government arm, *cometh* already rendering the verb. 1TH.5.12 proistamenous hymon -> *are over* / *you* keeps *over* inside the participle's unit and leaves the genitive a bare *you*, because *over* is the only word carrying the sense of proistemi and rule 17 forbids heading the unit on the copula *are*.

The hortatory *let us* frame rides with the subjunctive as a rule 7 and 9 helper - 1TH.5.6 katheudomen -> *let us ... sleep* and gregoromen -> *let us watch* - but where the Greek expresses the subject pronoun the *us* is that pronoun's and only *let* goes to the verb: 1TH.5.8 gives *us* to hemeis and the discontinuous *let ... be sober* to nephomen. A second coordinated subjunctive does not repeat the frame and keeps only its own *be*, as 1TH.5.6 nephomen -> *be sober* does.

report: Cross-verse: no genuine split. All 30 candidate groups reduce to the ASV rendering one word differently or to a difference the source licenses. Checked hardest: articles (5.3 unrepresented before a determinerless *travail* vs 5.4 aligned to a supplied *that* under rule 60; 5.9 empty before a bare *God* vs 5.23 aligned in *the God of peace*); substantival article + participle (5.7, 5.12, 5.24 split the pronoun off, 5.10 gives its single *who* to the article, which is rule 90's own word-count test and not a second analysis); negation (5.1 splits *no need*, chreia being a noun and the ASV writing two words; 5.15 joins me+tis to *none* under rule 59; 5.5 keeps *not* on ouk because oude carries its own *nor*; 5.3 keeps *in no wise* whole under rule 33); supplied copula (5.18 to the demonstrative subject under rule 68, 5.24 to the predicate adjective and 5.28 to the preposition under rule 53 - three arms of one chain).

The one construction analysed two ways is a compound verb governing a bare case. 5.3 ephistatai autois -> *cometh* / *upon them* hands the preposition to the dative under rule 106's case-government arm; 5.12 proistamenous hymon -> *are over* / *you* keeps it with the participle. The difference is licensed and not a split: in 5.12 the ASV writes no verb word besides the copula, so stripping *over* would leave a unit headed on *are*, which rule 17 forbids. Recorded as a convention and promoted as an amendment to rule 106, whose arm states no such precondition although all three of its cited precedents (MRK.14.65, ACT.4.1, ACT.4.3) do have an English verb word of their own.

The candidate table is blind to `added`, so I read the dump for a fold/added split. The chapter has zero `added` units and every supplied word that could have been one has a licensing token present: *do* on loipoi (5.6, rule 56, hedged against rule 103 in its own note), *since* on the participle ontes (5.8, rule 86), *that* on the subordinating me (5.15, rule 40), *it* on poiesei (5.24, rule 7), *that* on the two infinitives expanded into finite clauses (5.1, 5.27, rule 85). No unlicensed clause-introducer anywhere, so no split hides behind the table.

BSB disagreements: neither is an error. echousei (5.3) is a convention difference - the ASV's *with child* is exhausted by en and gastri, and rule 94 forbids a three-token compound unit over two English words, so the participle of the idiom has no word left; the competing single-unit reading is already named in that unit's note, and BSB renders the participle because it writes *a pregnant woman*. de (5.21) is a text difference: the ASV's base omits the connective, as its own margin says, so it is rule 97's mirror case. Patched to say so; the edge is untouched.

Residual, left as the verse pass took it and hedged in-unit under rule 16: the head of hyperekperissou (5.13) -> *exceeding highly*, taken on *exceeding*. If a later pass queries the lemma, EPH.3.20 *exceeding abundantly* is the unit that would settle it, and *highly* would win if the corpus spends the root word there. Not worth an evidence round for one head; the same applies to oligopsychous (5.14) -> *faint hearted*, headed on *faint*.
